patterns: why is infinity minus infinity undefined
entries.answer: Infinity is not a number in the sense that a count of things is a number, and that is why it behaves so differently from everything else. It is a symbol for a process that keeps going rather than an amount you could arrive at, and every ordinary arithmetic rule breaks when one of its sides is infinite. That is why half of infinity is still infinity while any finite number divided by infinity is zero, and why infinity minus infinity is not zero but undefined. The two infinities people meet in maths are different from each other as well: counting to infinity gives a countable one, while the points on a line cannot be listed, which is a real distinction rather than a pedantic one. The useful picture is that infinity is a direction rather than a place, and it is not bigger than every number the way a mountain is bigger than a hill, it simply has no end.

entries.answer: Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, and the remarkable fact is that the same number comes out for every circle of every size, which is already unusual. It is also irrational, meaning it never repeats and never ends, and it is not the sort of number that has a fraction that describes it exactly, so it can only ever be written out approximately. The digits have been calculated to trillions of places and the most useful facts about them are the ones about their distribution rather than the digits themselves: they are statistically random-looking, which is why the digits of pi can be used as a source for the practical test of whether a sequence of numbers is random. Finding a genuinely new formula for it carries an unusual prize, and that says as much about how little we understand it as about the number.

entries.answer: Base ten is the counting system we use because we have ten fingers, and almost everything else about our numbers follows from that choice rather than from arithmetic. Multiplication, place value and the standard written forms are all consequences of it, and so is the way a number is read left to right as powers of ten. A different base changes all of that without changing any of the maths: in base twelve the same quantity is written differently and the multiplication table is easier, which is why a dozen is a convenient unit, while binary has only two digits and is the reason a computer is built from ones and zeroes. The honest summary is that ten is not better than any other base, it is simply the one our bodies made obvious, and the rules a person learns in school are efficient for ten and awkward for anything else.
